claims.claim: Cummins says the ethnograph model admits both the voices of the anthropologist and of the people being studied.
claims.source: Elizabeth Cummins, Understanding Ursula K. Le Guin (1990)
claims.quote: both the voices of the anthropologist

claims.claim: Cummins says Le Guin uses an omniscient point of view for the section covering ages seven to nineteen.
claims.source: Elizabeth Cummins, Understanding Ursula K. Le Guin (1990)
claims.quote: Le Guin uses an omniscient point of view

claims.claim: Bittner says fantastic narratives include 'documents' to create an air of factuality.
claims.source: James W. Bittner, Approaches to the Fiction of Ursula K. Le Guin (1984)
claims.quote: to create an air of factuality

claims.claim: Bittner describes the narrator of 'Winter's King' as a historian telling a familiar story.
claims.source: James W. Bittner, Approaches to the Fiction of Ursula K. Le Guin (1984)
claims.quote: The narrator is a historian, telling a familiar story

claims.claim: Bittner reports that the documents following Estraven's death include a hearth-tale from the archives of the College of Historians in Erhenrang.
claims.source: James W. Bittner, Approaches to the Fiction of Ursula K. Le Guin (1984)
claims.quote: archives of the College of Historians in Erhenrang

claims.claim: Bittner says the novel interleaves extracts from Estraven's journal with an anthropological report and Gethenian legends.
claims.source: James W. Bittner, Approaches to the Fiction of Ursula K. Le Guin (1984)
claims.quote: an anthropological report, and Gethenian legends

claims.claim: Slusser says the landscape of one of Le Guin's worlds is quite ordinary by earth standards.
claims.source: George Edgar Slusser, The Farthest Shores of Ursula K. Le Guin (Borgo Press, 1976)
claims.quote: The landscape is quite ordinary by earth standards

claims.claim: Slusser describes a narrative framework intermingled with interpolated tales, documents and diaries.
claims.source: George Edgar Slusser, The Farthest Shores of Ursula K. Le Guin (1976)
claims.quote: intermingled with interpolated tales, documents, diaries

claims.claim: An essay in Bloom's volume says Le Guin's style has evolved towards simplicity.
claims.source: An essay in Harold Bloom, ed., Ursula K. Le Guin: Modern Critical Views (Chelsea House, 1986) — contributor not resolvable from the snippet window
claims.quote: Le Guin's style has evolved towards simplicity

claims.claim: Bloom says the narrator of that chapter is a field investigator of the Ekumen wryly cataloging a weird matter.
claims.source: Harold Bloom, introduction to Ursula K. Le Guin: Modern Critical Views (Chelsea House, 1986)

claims.claim: An essay in Bloom's volume says three chapters and the Appendix are documents separate from the actual narrative.
claims.source: An essay in Harold Bloom, ed., Ursula K. Le Guin: Modern Critical Views (1986)
claims.quote: are documents separate from the actual narrative

claims.claim: Bloom says the investigator's field notes add a number of sharper observations.
claims.source: Harold Bloom, introduction to Ursula K. Le Guin's The Left Hand of Darkness (Chelsea House, 1987)
claims.quote: Her field notes add a number of sharper observations

claims.claim: Cadden says much of Le Guin's short fiction shows a steady use of free indirect discourse.
claims.source: Mike Cadden, Ursula K. Le Guin Beyond Genre: Fiction for Children and Adults (Routledge, 2005)
claims.quote: a steady use of free indirect discourse

claims.claim: Cadden calls 'A Description of Earthsea' a text that is neither story nor afterword.
claims.source: Mike Cadden, Ursula K. Le Guin Beyond Genre (Routledge, 2005)
claims.quote: a text that is neither story nor afterword

claims.claim: Cadden says 'A Description of Earthsea' runs to almost thirty pages of Earthsea lore and history.
claims.source: Mike Cadden, Ursula K. Le Guin Beyond Genre (Routledge, 2005)
claims.quote: almost thirty pages of Earthsea lore and history
